title: Orientation and toolkit
why: Every later module assumes you can use a terminal, version your work with git, debug C, rebuild a Python environment and read papers efficiently. Set this up once here so it does not slow you down later. The repo you create holds every module's work.

steps.title: Missing Semester 2020, Lecture 1: Course overview + the shell
steps.detail: Windows users: install WSL2 first (next step) and work inside it. Do the exercises at the bottom of the page.

steps.title: Install WSL2 (Windows only)
steps.detail: Run `wsl --install`, then keep your course files inside the Linux filesystem (~/), not /mnt/c, or builds will be slow. macOS users: install Xcode Command Line Tools and Homebrew instead.

steps.title: Missing Semester 2020, Lecture 2: Shell Tools and Scripting
steps.detail: Focus on pipes, find, grep and writing a small bash script with set -euo pipefail. Later modules use scripts like this for benchmark sweeps.

steps.title: Missing Semester 2020, Lecture 3: Editors (Vim)
steps.detail: You do not need to switch to Vim. Learn enough to edit files over ssh on a remote machine, and set up your main editor with clangd and a Python language server.

steps.title: Missing Semester 2020, Lecture 6: Version Control (Git)
steps.detail: Understand the data model (blobs, trees, commits, refs) rather than memorizing commands.

steps.title: Learn Git Branching: Main tab Introduction Sequence, Remote tab first two levels
steps.detail: Interactive drills for commit, branch, merge, rebase and remotes. Then use one branch per module and tag each finished module.

steps.title: Pro Git, ch. 2 Git Basics, ch. 3 Git Branching, sections 7.3 Stashing and 7.10 Debugging with Git
steps.detail: Use as a reference when something goes wrong. Learn git log --oneline --graph, git stash and git bisect.

steps.title: Missing Semester 2020, Lecture 7: Debugging and Profiling
steps.detail: Covers printf debugging, gdb and pdb, perf and flame graphs. Modules 1-3 use all of these.

steps.title: C toolchain + debugger: GDB docs or the LLDB tutorial
steps.detail: Install clang (or gcc) and make. Compile a buggy program with -g -O0 -fsanitize=address, then set a breakpoint, step, print a variable and get a backtrace. Linux users can use gdb instead (https://www.gnu.org/software/gdb/documentation/).

steps.title: Python environment with uv (or venv)
steps.detail: Create one project environment with numpy, matplotlib, pytest and torch (the CPU build is enough). Commit uv.lock or requirements.txt.

steps.title: S. Keshav, How to Read a Paper
steps.detail: A short paper. Use the three-pass method on each paper in this course and keep a one-paragraph summary per paper in your repo.

steps.title: Julia Evans, How to ask good questions
steps.detail: Before asking anyone for help, write down what you tried, the exact error and a minimal reproduction.

steps.title: Join the GPU MODE community
steps.detail: A Discord server for GPU kernel and ML systems work; its talks are also on YouTube. Read the pinned messages before posting.

steps.title: Start a learning log (Julia Evans, Get your work recognized: write a brag document)
steps.detail: Keep LOG.md in your repo with one dated entry per session: what you did, what confused you, what you will do next. Write a short public post at the end of each module.

build: A public GitHub repo `ml-compilers-log` with a README (goals, schedule, hardware), LOG.md, a modules/ directory, a Makefile target that compiles and runs a sanitized C hello-world, a pytest that passes, and a GitHub Actions CI workflow that runs both on every push.
check: Write a one-line shell pipeline that prints the 5 largest files under a directory.
Explain the difference between a commit, a branch and a tag in git's data model.
Use gdb or lldb to find the line of a segfault in a 20-line C program without adding printfs.
Recreate your Python environment from scratch on a clean machine (or container) from your lockfile alone.
Summarize a paper after Keshav's first pass in five sentences (the five Cs).
outcomes: Write shell pipelines and small bash scripts, locally and over ssh.
Use git branches and tags, and recover from a bad merge with git reflog.
Compile C with -g and -fsanitize=address and find a crash with gdb or lldb.
Rebuild your Python environment from a lockfile.
Read a paper with Keshav's three-pass method and write a five-sentence summary.
stuck: WSL slow or files missing: keep the repo under ~/ in Linux, not /mnt/c; open it with `code .` from WSL.
macOS 'gdb' won't run: use lldb, which ships with the Xcode Command Line Tools; the commands map almost one to one (lldb's GDB-to-LLDB command map helps).
git 'detached HEAD' or a messy merge: run `git status` and `git log --oneline --graph --all` before anything else; `git reflog` can recover almost anything.
Limit tooling setup (dotfiles, themes) to two evenings, then start Module 1.
Pip and conda in the same env cause mysterious import errors: pick one tool (uv recommended) and one env per project.

project.title: Public course repo + first blog post
project.brief: Set up the repository that will hold every module's work and portfolio project for the whole course, with CI from day one. Publish a first blog post (GitHub Pages, a personal site, or similar) titled something like 'Why I'm building an ML compiler from scratch', stating your goals, your starting point, and a dated plan for the course.
deliverables: repo with README, LOG.md, Makefile, a sanitized C test and a pytest, all green in GitHub Actions
a short CONTRIBUTING-style note to yourself: branch-per-module, commit message conventions, how to tag a finished module
a 600–1000 word blog post on your goals and plan, linked from the README

rubric.solid: CI passes on push; README states the plan; LOG.md has at least 3 dated entries; blog post is published and linked.
rubric.exceptional: Reproducible environment (uv.lock or a devcontainer) that CI builds from scratch, and a `make bench` target that writes timings to CSV for use in later modules.

title: C, properly
why: The compiler you build later emits C, so you must read and write it without hesitation. Pointers, arrays, structs, the heap and the build toolchain underlie every later kernel.

steps.title: CS50x 2026 Week 1: C
steps.detail: Watch at 1.5x if you already program. Focus on compiling with clang, types and printf format specifiers.

steps.title: CS50x Problem Set 1: Mario (more comfortable) and Credit
steps.detail: Do the 'more comfortable' versions; they need nested loops and integer digit arithmetic.

steps.title: CS50x 2026 Week 2: Arrays
steps.detail: Focus on strings as char arrays ending in '\0', and on argc/argv.

steps.title: CS50x Problem Set 2: Caesar (or Substitution)
steps.detail: Implement it, then rebuild with -fsanitize=address and introduce an out-of-bounds read to see what ASan reports.

steps.title: CS50x 2026 Week 4: Memory
steps.detail: Pointers, malloc/free, stack vs heap, valgrind. Watch all of it.

steps.title: Beej's Guide to C, ch. 5-7: Pointers (Cower In Fear!), Arrays, Strings
steps.detail: Type out each example and predict its output before running it.

steps.title: Beej's Guide to C, ch. 8 Structs, ch. 11 Pointers II: Arithmetic, ch. 12 Manual Memory Allocation
steps.detail: Pointer arithmetic here is the same idea as tensor strides in Module 6.

steps.title: CS50x Problem Set 4: Filter (less comfortable) and Recover
steps.detail: Filter is 2-D array indexing over pixels; Recover is raw byte I/O with fread. Do both.

steps.title: CS50x 2026 Week 5: Data Structures
steps.detail: Linked lists, trees and hash tables built from structs and pointers.

steps.title: CS50x Problem Set 5: Speller
steps.detail: Write the hash table. valgrind must report zero leaks; compare your timing against the staff solution.

steps.title: Build Your Own Lisp, ch. 6-10 (Parsing through Q-Expressions)
steps.detail: Chapters 6 Parsing through 10 Q-Expressions, including the bonus marks. This is your first tree-walking interpreter.

build: (1) Build Your Own Lisp through ch. 10 Q-Expressions, with a REPL that evaluates (eval (head {(+ 1 2) 3})). (2) A generic open-addressing hash map in C (string keys, void* values, resize at 0.7 load) plus a test file inserting 1M keys, compiled with -Wall -Wextra -fsanitize=address,undefined and running clean.
check: Draw stack and heap for a function that mallocs an int array, returns it and the caller frees it.
Explain why sizeof(arr) differs inside and outside a function that receives arr.
Explain p[i], *(p+i) and i[p], and what pointer arithmetic does on an int* vs a char*.
Speller passes check50 and valgrind reports 0 bytes lost.
ASan and UBSan are silent on your hash map test.

extra.title: cstack, Let's Build a Simple Database, parts 1-8

outcomes: Write multi-file C programs with pointers, structs and malloc/free that run clean under ASan, UBSan and valgrind.
Implement a hash table in C and draw its memory layout.
Build a tree-walking interpreter (parser plus evaluator) in C.
Build every C project with make and -Wall -Wextra -g -fsanitize=address,undefined.
stuck: Returning a pointer to a local array: the array lives in the returning function's stack frame and is invalid after return. Re-watch the stack vs heap part of CS50 Week 4.
sizeof on an array parameter gives the pointer size, because the array decays to a pointer when passed. Pass the length explicitly (Beej ch. 6 Arrays).
Off-by-one on strings: allocate strlen(s)+1 for the terminating '\0'.
A bug that disappears when you add printf is usually undefined behaviour. Build with -Wall -Wextra -g -fsanitize=address,undefined while developing.
mpc parse errors are hard to read: print the AST with mpc_ast_print before debugging your evaluator.

project.title: An arena-allocated tensor runtime core in C
project.brief: Write a small C library `tcore` that stores N-dimensional float32 tensors (shape, strides, offset, data) in an arena allocator, with elementwise add and mul, a naive matmul and a C test suite. Your compiler's generated C will link against it later. Benchmark creating and freeing 10^4, 10^5 and 10^6 tensors of 16, 256 and 4096 floats with the arena vs malloc/free, and explain the difference.
deliverables: repo with tcore.h/tcore.c, a Makefile, and tests that run clean under ASan, UBSan and valgrind
README with a table and plot of allocation throughput (arena vs malloc) across tensor counts and sizes
a 600–1200 word write-up explaining your memory layout, ownership rules, and why arenas suit compiler-generated code

rubric.solid: All tests pass under sanitizers with zero leaks; arena benchmark reported with at least 3 sizes and repeated runs; API documented in the header.
rubric.exceptional: Randomized property tests that compare tcore results against NumPy, benchmark results reported as median and interquartile range, and CI that runs the sanitizer build on every push.

title: How machines run code
why: Bits, two's complement, IEEE floats, x86-64 and the stack: the first half of CMU 15-213. You need to read the machine code your compiler's output becomes.

steps.title: CMU 15-213 F15 Lectures 2-3: Bits, Bytes and Integers
steps.detail: Videos are in the 15-213 F15 Panopto folder (see extras). Focus on two's complement, casting and overflow.

steps.title: Dive into Systems ch. 4: Binary and Data Representation
steps.detail: Do the inline exercises, especially signed/unsigned conversion.

steps.title: CS:APP Data Lab: all puzzles
steps.detail: Get datalab-handout from the labs page. Solve every bit and float puzzle within the op limits; run ./btest and ./dlc until both pass.

steps.title: CMU 15-213 F15 Lecture 4: Floating Point
steps.detail: Sign, exponent and fraction fields, denormals, rounding, and why float addition is not associative. Module 3 and the reduction kernels later depend on the last point.

steps.title: CMU 15-213 F15 Lectures 5-6: Machine-Level Programming I-II (Basics, Control)
steps.detail: Then 06-machine-control.pdf. Registers, mov, lea, condition codes, jumps, loops.

steps.title: Dive into Systems ch. 7: x86-64 Assembly, sections 7.1-7.6
steps.detail: Read 7.1 Assembly Basics through 7.6 Recursion and paste each example into Compiler Explorer.

steps.title: CMU 15-213 F15 Lectures 7-9: Procedures, Data, Advanced
steps.detail: Then 08-machine-data.pdf and 09-machine-advanced.pdf. Stack frames, calling convention, arrays/structs layout, buffer overflow.

steps.title: Compiler Explorer: compile your Module 1 functions
steps.detail: Compare -O0 and -O2 for a sum loop, a struct field access and a recursive function. Annotate the -O2 asm by hand.

steps.title: CS:APP Bomb Lab: phases 1-6
steps.detail: Use gdb (break, stepi, x/s, info registers) and objdump -d. For each phase, note which C construct it encodes (comparison, loop, switch, recursion, linked list).

steps.title: cpu.land ch. 1-5: The Basics through The Translator in Your Computer
steps.detail: Chapters 1 The Basics, 2 Slice Dat Time, 3 How to Run a Program, 4 Becoming an Elf-Lord, 5 The Translator in Your Computer: syscalls, interrupts, exec, ELF and paging.

build: Defuse all six Bomb Lab phases (plus the secret phase if you find it). Then write half a page explaining the System V AMD64 calling convention: argument registers, return value, caller- vs callee-saved registers, stack alignment, red zone, illustrated with godbolt output of a 7-argument function.
check: Data Lab: btest passes every puzzle and dlc reports no op-count violations.
Bomb Lab: all 6 phases defused without an explosion (phases 1-4 are worth 10 points each, 5-6 are worth 15).
Explain why (int)(unsigned)-1 and -1 > 0u behave as they do.
Explain why 0.1+0.2 != 0.3 and why summing floats in a different order changes the result.
Given a 10-line asm function, write the C that produced it.

extra.title: 15-213 F15 lecture videos (Panopto folder)
extra.note: The recorded lectures matching the slides above.

extra.title: Pete Kivolowitz, Assembly Language Programming for ARM64
extra.note: If you are on Apple Silicon.

outcomes: Read compiler-generated x86-64 assembly and write the C it came from.
Predict the result of signed/unsigned casts, integer overflow and float rounding cases.
Name the System V AMD64 argument, return and callee-saved registers, and inspect them in gdb.
Describe the steps from source file to running process: compile, link, load, exec.
stuck: Bomb Lab: do not guess. Disassemble with `objdump -d` and use gdb `break explode_bomb` first so a wrong answer never detonates.
AT&T vs Intel syntax confusion (operand order is reversed): pick one, and set Compiler Explorer and gdb (`set disassembly-flavor intel`) to match.
Data Lab op-count limits: build masks with shifts and ~, and check each step's bit pattern in a scratch C program before using it.
Floating point: 0.1 cannot be represented exactly; work through the rounding examples in Lecture 4 by hand rather than trusting intuition.
At -O0 the asm is verbose and stack-heavy; compare -O0 vs -O2 in Compiler Explorer to see what the optimizer actually does.

project.title: Compiler Explorer study: what -O2 does to tensor loops
project.brief: Pick five small kernels you will meet later (axpy, dot product, a strided gather, a reduction with a float accumulator, a 3x3 conv inner loop). For each, compile with clang and gcc at -O0/-O2/-O3 (and -ffast-math for the reductions), read the assembly, and document which optimizations happened: vectorization, unrolling, strength reduction, and why the float reduction does not vectorize without fast-math. Time each variant.
deliverables: repo with the kernels, a script that regenerates annotated assembly and timings
README with a table of cycles/element per kernel, compiler and flag, plus annotated asm snippets
a 600–1200 word write-up explaining floating-point associativity, aliasing (restrict) and their effect on vectorization

rubric.solid: All 5 kernels x 2 compilers x 3+ flag sets timed with repeated runs; each asm snippet annotated with what each block does.
rubric.exceptional: Uses `perf stat` or llvm-mca to explain throughput from instruction counts and port pressure, demonstrates a measurable speedup from adding `restrict` or reassociation, and predicts the speedup before measuring it.

title: Memory and caches
why: Cache lines, locality and TLBs explain why loop order changes runtime. Tiling, fusion and vectorization decisions later in the course depend on this module.

steps.title: CMU 15-213 F15 Lecture 11: The Memory Hierarchy
steps.detail: Locality, the latency pyramid, why caches work.

steps.title: CMU 15-213 F15 Lecture 12: Cache Memories
steps.detail: Sets, ways and lines, miss classification, and the matmul loop-order analysis at the end. This is the core lecture of the module.

steps.title: Dive into Systems ch. 11: Storage and the Memory Hierarchy, sections 11.3-11.5
steps.detail: Read 11.3 Locality, 11.4 Caching and 11.5 Cache Analysis and Cachegrind; do the cache-mapping exercises.

steps.title: Igor Ostrovsky, Gallery of Processor Cache Effects: all 7 examples
steps.detail: Reproduce each in C on your machine and plot it. Mark where your L1, L2 and L3 sizes appear.

steps.title: Drepper, What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory, §3 CPU Caches and §6.2 Cache Access
steps.detail: Skip §2 (DRAM hardware) and §4-5. §6.2 has the tiled matmul with measured speedups.

steps.title: CS:APP Cache Lab Part A: cache simulator
steps.detail: Write csim.c that replays valgrind traces with LRU; match csim-ref on all test traces.

steps.title: CS:APP Cache Lab Part B: optimized transpose
steps.detail: Blocked transpose for 32x32 (<300 misses), 64x64 (<1300) and 61x67 (<2000). This is your first hand-written schedule.

steps.title: CMU 15-213 F15 Lecture 17: Virtual Memory Concepts
steps.detail: Pages, page tables and the TLB; why large strides cause TLB misses.

steps.title: Algorithms for Modern Hardware: RAM & CPU Caches chapter
steps.detail: Read Memory Bandwidth, Memory Latency, Cache Lines, Cache Associativity and AoS and SoA; run two of the benchmarks.

build: Reproduce Ostrovsky's seven effects with plots. Then time naive C matmul at N=1024 in all six loop orders (ijk, ikj, jik, jki, kij, kji) at -O2, plot GFLOP/s, and write a page explaining the ranking with per-iteration miss counts (as in Lecture 12). Add a tiled version and report its speedup.
check: Explain why ikj beats ijk, with misses-per-inner-iteration arithmetic.
Cache Lab: test-csim gives full marks, and transpose has fewer than 300 misses on 32x32, 1300 on 64x64 and 2000 on 61x67.
Given a 32 KB 8-way cache with 64 B lines, compute sets and the address bits for tag/index/offset.
Explain conflict misses and why padding a 4096-wide array can help.
Point to your L1/L2/L3 transitions on the Ostrovsky array-size plot.

extra.title: Fabian Giesen, Why do CPUs have multiple cache levels?

outcomes: Compute expected cache misses per inner-loop iteration for a loop nest, given the cache geometry.
Speed up a memory-bound kernel with loop reordering and tiling, and measure the speedup.
Read your machine's L1, L2 and L3 sizes off a measured latency plot.
Use perf stat cache-miss counters to confirm or reject a performance hypothesis.
stuck: Timings are noisy: warm up, repeat, report the median, pin to a core, and do not run with a browser open on a laptop on battery.
Cache Lab 64x64 transpose: 8x8 blocking, which works for 32x32, gets conflict misses here because rows 4 apart map to the same sets. Split each 8x8 block into 4x4 sub-blocks.
Apple Silicon and some laptops lack perf: use Instruments or measure on a Linux box/cloud VM; the concepts transfer.
The compiler may optimize your benchmark away; consume the result (print a checksum) and check the asm.
Bandwidth-bound vs latency-bound: a sequential scan is limited by bandwidth, a pointer chase by latency. Ostrovsky's Example 1 and Example 4 separate the two.

project.title: Single-core CPU SGEMM: from naive to a large fraction of peak
project.brief: Starting from your naive C matmul, optimize single-threaded float32 GEMM for square N from 256 to 2048 step by step: loop order, cache tiling, register blocking with a micro-kernel, SIMD (AVX2/NEON intrinsics or auto-vectorization) and packing. Compute your core's theoretical peak (FMA units x SIMD width x 2 x clock) and plot each version's GFLOP/s as a fraction of it, next to OpenBLAS or Accelerate restricted to one thread.
deliverables: repo with each optimization step as its own function or commit, a correctness test against a reference, and a benchmark script
README with a GFLOP/s vs N plot for all versions and the BLAS baseline, and your peak-FLOPs calculation
a 600–1200 word write-up explaining which step removed which bottleneck, backed by cache-miss counts or a roofline argument

rubric.solid: At least 5 versions, each correct; best version reaches at least 30% of single-core peak; all numbers are medians with the CPU model stated.
rubric.exceptional: Best version reaches at least 60% of peak or within 2x of single-threaded OpenBLAS, includes a roofline plot, and the write-up attributes each speedup with perf miss counts or FLOPs per byte.

references.title: Simon Boehm, Fast Multidimensional Matrix Multiplication on CPU from Scratch
Algorithms for Modern Hardware: Matrix Multiplication

title: Linear algebra
why: Tensors are the data and matmul is the main workload. You need matrices both as transformations and as computations (elimination and factorization).

steps.title: 3Blue1Brown Essence of Linear Algebra ch. 1-4: Vectors, Linear combinations/span, Linear transformations, Matrix multiplication
steps.detail: Also watch the span and matrix-multiplication lessons. Goal: read a matrix's columns as where the basis vectors land.

steps.title: 3Blue1Brown ch. 6-7: Determinant, Inverse matrices / column space / null space
steps.detail: Then watch the inverse matrices lesson.

steps.title: 3Blue1Brown ch. 9, 13-14: Dot products, Change of basis, Eigenvectors
steps.detail: Then the change of basis and eigenvectors lessons. Skip cross products.

steps.title: MIT 18.06SC Lecture 1: The Geometry of Linear Equations
steps.detail: Watch the lecture, then do the session's problem set and check against the solutions.

steps.title: MIT 18.06SC Lectures 2-3: Elimination with Matrices; Multiplication and Inverse Matrices
steps.detail: Then multiplication-and-inverse-matrices/. Lecture 3 covers four ways to multiply matrices (row, column, columns times rows, blocks), which map to different kernel loop orders.

steps.title: MIT 18.06SC Lecture 4: Factorization into A = LU
steps.detail: Count the operations and confirm elimination costs about n^3/3 multiply-adds.

steps.title: MIT 18.06SC Lecture 5: Transposes, Permutations, Vector Spaces
steps.detail: Permutation matrices reappear as tensor permute in Module 6.

steps.title: MIT 18.06SC Lectures 6, 10: Column Space and Nullspace; The Four Fundamental Subspaces
steps.detail: Then the-four-fundamental-subspaces/. Do both problem sets.

steps.title: PyTorch blog, Inside the Matrix: Visualizing Matrix Multiplication
steps.detail: Read sections 2 and 3 (dot product, matrix-vector, summed outer products, expressions). Leave section 4 onward (attention) for Module 9.

steps.title: Pure-Python linear algebra library
steps.detail: Implement it as specified in build; use numpy.linalg only as the oracle in tests.

build: Pure-Python (lists only) matmul, transpose, LU decomposition with partial pivoting, forward/back substitution and solve(A,b). Test against numpy on 100 random matrices to 1e-9, and include a 4-ways-of-matmul file (row, column, outer-product, block) that all agree.
check: Explain matrix multiplication as composition of transformations, and as a sum of outer products.
Explain what the determinant means geometrically and why det=0 means no inverse.
Perform LU by hand on a 3x3 and verify L*U=A.
State the dimensions of the four fundamental subspaces of an m x n matrix of rank r.
Count the flops of an n x n matmul and of LU.

extra.title: MIT 18.06SC Unit II: Least squares, determinants, eigenvalues

outcomes: Compute a matmul four ways (row, column, outer product, block) and say which access pattern each uses.
Implement LU with partial pivoting and use it to solve Ax=b.
State the rank, null space dimension and determinant meaning for a given small matrix.
Measure relative error against NumPy and show a case where pivoting changes it.
stuck: The 3Blue1Brown videos give intuition, not fluency. Work the 18.06SC problem sets by hand.
LU without pivoting fails on a zero (or tiny) pivot; test on [[1e-20,1],[1,1]] to see catastrophic error, then add pivoting.
Comparing floats with == in tests: use a relative tolerance (numpy.allclose semantics).
Mixing up row-major indexing A[i][j] with the column picture of Ax: write out a 2x2 example both ways (18.06 Lecture 1).

project.title: Blocked matrix algorithms and the cost of numerical stability
project.brief: In NumPy, implement blocked matmul and right-looking blocked LU that only call matmul on tiles. For N = 256, 512, 1024 and 2048 and block sizes 32, 64 and 128, compare speed and accuracy against your unblocked versions and scipy.linalg.lu. Measure backward error ||PA-LU||/||A|| against condition number (1 to 1e12), with and without pivoting, and relate the blocking to the cache tiling of Module 3.
deliverables: repo with blocked matmul and LU, tests against numpy.linalg on random and ill-conditioned matrices
README with plots: runtime vs N vs block size, and backward error vs condition number for each variant
a 600–1200 word write-up explaining why blocked algorithms map to matmul (and therefore to GPUs), with your measurements

rubric.solid: Blocked LU matches scipy.linalg.lu to 1e-10 on well-conditioned inputs; plots for at least 3 block sizes; pivoting failure case demonstrated.
rubric.exceptional: Adds Cholesky or QR, shows growth-factor results on Wilkinson's matrix, and reports a measured speedup from tuning block size.

title: Calculus and gradients
why: Autodiff is the chain rule applied mechanically. Learn it by hand on scalars first, then for vectors and matrices, because your compiler will generate backward passes.

steps.title: 3Blue1Brown, Essence of Calculus ch. 1-2: The essence of calculus; The paradox of the derivative
steps.detail: Chapter 2 is the next lesson, /lessons/derivatives.

steps.title: 3Blue1Brown, Essence of Calculus ch. 3-4: Derivative formulas through geometry; Visualizing the chain rule and product rule
steps.detail: Chapter 3 is /lessons/derivatives-power-rule. Pause on the chain rule section and redo it on paper for sin(x^2).

steps.title: Karpathy, Hacker's guide to Neural Networks, Chapter 1: Real-valued Circuits
steps.detail: Code the add, multiply and sigmoid gates with forward and backward in Python, then check each against a numerical gradient.

steps.title: Parr & Howard, The Matrix Calculus You Need For Deep Learning: Introduction through Generalization of the Jacobian
steps.detail: Covers the scalar rule review, partial derivatives, and the Jacobian. Work the Jacobian examples by hand.

steps.title: Parr & Howard: element-wise binary operators, scalar expansion, vector sum reduction, the chain rules
steps.detail: The sum-reduction and scalar-expansion results are the backward rules for sum and expand in your autograd.

steps.title: Parr & Howard: the gradient of neuron activation and of the neural network loss function
steps.detail: Derive dL/dW and dL/db for one linear+ReLU layer and check them numerically.

steps.title: Sasha Rush, Autodiff Puzzles: all puzzles
steps.detail: Open the Colab notebook from the README. Each problem gives a tensor function (id, cosine, mean, cumsum, sort, matmul, 2D conv, and others); you write its derivative and the notebook tests it.

steps.title: Gradient check harness
steps.detail: Write gradcheck(f, x) in NumPy using the centered difference, float64 and relative error as the CS231n notes describe. Use it on your matmul, softmax and log-softmax derivations.

build: Finish all Autodiff Puzzles. Then write one NumPy file with forward and backward for matmul, sum(axis), broadcast add, ReLU, softmax and cross-entropy, each passing your gradcheck at relative error below 1e-6 in float64.
check: Derive the derivative of sigmoid and write it in terms of sigmoid itself.
For C = A @ B, write dL/dA and dL/dB in terms of dL/dC, with shapes.
Show why the gradient of a broadcast is a sum over the broadcast axes, using a (3,) + (2,3) example.
Derive why softmax followed by cross-entropy has gradient p - y with respect to the logits.
All Autodiff Puzzles pass in the notebook.

extra.title: MIT 18.S096 Matrix Calculus for Machine Learning and Beyond (IAP 2023)
extra.note: Lectures 1-3 treat derivatives as linear operators, Jacobians, and finite-difference checks.

extra.title: Chris Olah, Calculus on Computational Graphs: Backpropagation
extra.note: Forward-mode vs reverse-mode on a small graph.

outcomes: After this module you can derive gradients of matmul, softmax and cross-entropy with correct shapes.
After this module you can state when forward-mode autodiff is cheaper than reverse-mode, in terms of input and output counts.
After this module you can check any gradient with finite differences and locate which term is wrong.
After this module you can explain why the backward of a broadcast is a sum and the backward of a sum is a broadcast.
stuck: Shape errors: write the shape next to every term. dL/dA must have A's shape, which tells you where the transposes go.
Gradcheck stuck around 1e-3: use float64, centered differences, a step near 1e-5, and relative error. float32 will not reach 1e-6.
Softmax overflow: subtract the row max before exp. The gradient does not change.
ReLU gradcheck fails at 0 because ReLU is not differentiable there. Use inputs that are not within the step size of 0.

project.title: Forward-mode vs reverse-mode autodiff: implement both and measure
project.brief: Implement forward-mode AD with dual numbers and reverse-mode AD on a tape, over the same small expression language (scalar ops and NumPy arrays). Construct functions with n inputs and m outputs and measure time and memory as n and m vary, demonstrating the n-vs-m crossover; then compute a Hessian-vector product by composing the two (forward-over-reverse).
deliverables: repo with both AD modes, a shared gradcheck, and tests against PyTorch or JAX
README with plots of runtime and memory vs n and m for both modes, and the HVP verified against finite differences
a 600–1200 word write-up explaining JVPs, VJPs, why deep learning uses reverse mode, and what the tape costs in memory

rubric.solid: Both modes agree with PyTorch to 1e-8 in float64 on at least 10 test functions; crossover demonstrated in a plot.
rubric.exceptional: Implements HVP and uses it in a few steps of Newton-CG on a small problem, adds gradient checkpointing to the tape and plots the memory/compute trade-off, and relates the design to JAX's jvp/vjp.

title: Tensors, broadcasting, strides
why: A tensor is a pointer, a shape and strides. Reshape, permute and expand are pure index arithmetic, which is exactly what you will compile in Module 22.

steps.title: Rougier, From Python to NumPy, chapter "Anatomy of an array"
steps.detail: Sections: memory layout, views and copies. Run every snippet.

steps.title: Alex Riley (ajcr), An Illustrated Guide to Shape and Strides, parts 1-3
steps.detail: Part 2 (/stride-guide-part-2/) covers transpose and C vs Fortran order; part 3 (/stride-guide-part-3/) covers as_strided. Compute each stride by hand before printing it.

steps.title: Rougier, chapter "Code vectorization": Uniform vectorization
steps.detail: Do the Game of Life section. Skip temporal and spatial vectorization on the first pass.

steps.title: numpy-100 #1-40
steps.detail: No hints. Mark each one that relies on strides, broadcasting or views.

steps.title: Edward Yang, PyTorch internals, first part (tensors, strides, storage, dispatch, extension points)
steps.detail: The post is in two parts. Stop when it moves to working in the PyTorch codebase; the stride and storage diagrams are what you need here.

steps.title: Sasha Rush, Tensor Puzzles 1-10
steps.detail: ones, sum, outer, diag, eye, triu, cumsum, diff, vstack, roll. One line under 80 columns each, using only arange, where, @, arithmetic, comparisons, indexing and earlier puzzles.

steps.title: Sasha Rush, Tensor Puzzles 11-21
steps.detail: flip, compress, pad_to, sequence_mask, bincount, scatter_add, flatten, linspace, heaviside, repeat, bucketize.

steps.title: numpy-100 stride exercises: #75, #76, #81, #84, #87
steps.detail: Sliding-window averages, shifted rows, contiguous 3x3 blocks and 4x4 block sums. Solve each with numpy.lib.stride_tricks.as_strided and write down the strides you passed.

build: An NDArray class in pure Python over a flat list: shape, strides, offset; __getitem__ for ints and slices (views, no copy); reshape (view when contiguous, else copy), permute/transpose, expand (stride 0), broadcasting elementwise add/mul, sum(axis), and contiguous(). Tested against NumPy on random shapes.
check: Given a contiguous float32 array of shape (2,3,4), state its strides in bytes and the flat element index of [1,2,3].
Explain why transpose costs nothing but a reshape after it may need a copy.
Explain how expand is implemented with stride 0.
All 21 Tensor Puzzles pass.
Build a sliding-window view with as_strided and justify each stride.

extra.title: fast.ai Part 2, Lessons 11-12
extra.note: Lesson 11 builds matrix multiplication from scratch; lesson 12 is mean-shift clustering.

outcomes: After this module you can compute strides and offsets for any slice, transpose or expand and predict when an operation copies.
After this module you can implement broadcasting from its rules.
After this module you can replace Python loops with array operations using only broadcasting and indexing.
After this module you can explain how PyTorch separates a tensor's storage from its view metadata.
stuck: Negative-step slices: the offset moves to the last element and the stride becomes negative. Test x[::-1] early.
Reshape after transpose: the result usually cannot be described with strides, so it must copy. Detect this by comparing the strides with those of a contiguous array of the same shape.
Broadcasting aligns shapes from the right. (3,) + (3,1) gives (3,3), not an error.
Tensor Puzzles forbid sum and most library functions. After puzzle 2, reduce by reusing your own sum (for example a @ ones).

project.title: A view-tracking shape tracker (a mini ShapeTracker)
project.brief: Build a symbolic view system that composes reshape, permute, expand, pad, shrink and stride operations without touching data. It emits one index expression (a C string) mapping output index to input address, or reports that a copy is needed. This is the idea behind tinygrad's ShapeTracker, which you will meet again in the compiler modules. Property-test it against NumPy on random op chains.
deliverables: repo with the view system, a C-expression emitter, and a randomized property test against NumPy
README showing example op chains, their emitted index expressions, and how many chains merge into one view vs need a copy
a 600–1200 word write-up explaining when two views can be merged and why this lets a compiler fuse movement ops for free

rubric.solid: Passes at least 10,000 random chains of up to 6 ops against NumPy; emitted C compiles and gives identical results.
rubric.exceptional: Simplifies emitted index expressions (constant folding, removing mod/div when provably unneeded), supports masks for pad, and compares its design to tinygrad's ShapeTracker with references to specific code.

project.title: A tiny graph IR for your autograd: visualize, optimize, codegen
project.brief: Make your micrograd record an explicit graph IR, then write three passes over it: dead-code elimination, common-subexpression elimination, and a codegen pass that emits a straight-line Python (or C) function computing the forward and backward pass with no Value objects. Benchmark the generated code against the interpreted engine on an MLP. This is your first compiler.
deliverables: repo with the IR, the three passes, and tests that the generated code matches the interpreted gradients exactly
README with Graphviz renders before and after optimization and a speedup table vs the interpreted engine
a 600–1200 word write-up explaining tracing vs interpretation and what each pass removed, with node counts

rubric.solid: Generated code matches interpreted gradients bit-for-bit on random MLPs; reports node counts before/after each pass and a measured speedup.
rubric.exceptional: Generated C version gives a speedup of 100x or more over the interpreter, adds constant folding, and the write-up connects the design to torch.fx or jax.make_jaxpr.

project.title: A C inference engine for GPT-2 with KV cache, benchmarked
project.brief: Write a single-file C (or C with OpenMP) inference engine for GPT-2 124M that loads the weights you exported from NumPy, implements a KV cache, and generates text matching your NumPy reference token for token. Measure prefill and decode throughput, compare decode tokens/s against the memory-bandwidth bound you compute from model size, and add int8 weight-only quantization with a perplexity comparison.
deliverables: repo with the C engine, a weight-export script, and a test that greedy output matches the NumPy reference exactly
README with tokens/s for prefill and decode, with and without KV cache, fp32 vs int8, against the computed bandwidth roofline
a 600–1200 word write-up explaining why decode is memory-bound, what the KV cache saves, and the accuracy cost of quantization

rubric.solid: Greedy output matches the reference for 100+ tokens; KV cache gives a measured speedup that grows with sequence length; numbers reported with the hardware stated.
rubric.exceptional: Decode reaches at least 50% of the memory-bandwidth bound, int8 perplexity on a held-out text stays within 1–2% of fp32, and the code is clean enough to compare favourably with llama2.c's run.c.
